stages.title: Compressible aerodynamics
stages.hook: A fast jet can be heard well after it passes, and at one speed it seems to hit an invisible wall of drag. What changes in the air near and above the speed of sound?
explain: Air is compressible: its density changes when pressure changes. The effect is small below Mach 0.3 but grows as speed rises. Sound is a small pressure disturbance travelling at a = √(γRT), where γ = 1.4 for air, R = 287 J/(kg·K) and T is the absolute temperature. At 288.15 K (15 °C) a ≈ 340 m/s, and in the cold air at 11 km (216.65 K) a ≈ 295 m/s.

Mach number M = v ÷ a. The flow is subsonic for M < 1, transonic around M 0.8 to 1.2, supersonic above 1 and hypersonic above about 5. When air is brought to rest isentropically, its temperature rises to the total temperature T₀ = T(1 + 0.2M²) for γ = 1.4. In supersonic flow, disturbances cannot travel upstream, so the air meets the object suddenly through a shock wave.

A normal shock is a thin region where the flow goes from supersonic to subsonic, with a jump in pressure, density and temperature. For M₁ = 2 in air, the static pressure ratio is p₂/p₁ = 1 + (2γ/(γ+1))(M₁² − 1) = 4.5 and downstream M₂ ≈ 0.577. Total pressure falls across a shock, which is a source of wave drag. At subsonic speeds, the Prandtl-Glauert rule estimates compressibility effects: C_p = C_p0 ÷ √(1 − M²).

example.q: Find the speed of sound at 11 km altitude where T = 216.65 K (γ = 1.4, R = 287 J/(kg·K)). What is the Mach number of an airliner at 250 m/s?

analogies.sea: A fast boat makes a V-shaped bow wave because the waves cannot get ahead of it. A supersonic aircraft makes a conical shock for the same reason.
analogies.city: A crowd running down a corridor pushes those ahead of them in a sudden jam when it can't warn them in time.
analogies.sport: A whip's crack is a small shock wave.
analogies.nature: Thunder is the shock wave of lightning's sudden heating.

stages.mnemonic: Sound speed grows with the square root of temperature; M is v over a; shocks jump everything up.
terms: Flight speed divided by the local speed of sound.
A thin region where pressure, density and temperature jump abruptly.
The temperature air would reach if brought to rest, T₀ = T(1 + 0.2M²).
Drag caused by shock waves at transonic and supersonic speeds.
The flight Mach number at which the flow first reaches M = 1 somewhere on the body.

misc.wrong: The speed of sound is a fixed value of 340 m/s everywhere.
misc.right: The speed of sound depends on temperature: it is about 340 m/s at 15 °C and about 295 m/s at 11 km where air is colder. Mach number is relative to the local value.

stages.limits: The formulas here assume a perfect gas with γ = 1.4. At very high Mach numbers the air heats enough that γ changes and gas chemistry matters.

questions.q: After a normal shock, the flow is

Supersonic
Hypersonic

To make the aircraft heavier and steadier in gusts
To fit more seats into the cabin
To produce more lift at low speed alone

o: Mach 0.95
Mach 0.2
Mach 3
Mach 8
questions.why: Transonic flow occurs roughly between Mach 0.8 and 1.2, where subsonic and supersonic regions coexist.

rubric: faster than the speed of sound
questions.model: Pressure disturbances travel at the speed of sound, so when an aircraft is faster than that they cannot get ahead of it. The air in front is not warned and is forced to change suddenly through a shock wave.

panel.q: A pilot flying at a constant true airspeed climbs from sea level into colder air. What happens to the Mach number?
o: It increases because the speed of sound falls
It decreases because the speed of sound rises

panel.q: Why does total pressure fall across a shock even though no heat is added?
o: A shock is irreversible and increases entropy
The shock removes mass from the flow, lowering pressure
Shocks cool the gas, so total pressure drops
Total pressure never changes across a shock
panel.why: The abrupt compression is not isentropic, so some stagnation pressure is lost.

panel.q: Why can the local flow over a wing be supersonic even when the aircraft flies below Mach 1?
panel.model: Air speeds up over the curved upper surface, so the local speed can exceed the flight speed. If it reaches the local speed of sound before the aircraft reaches Mach 1, there are pockets of supersonic flow ended by weak shocks, which is the transonic regime.
panel.why: The critical Mach number is below 1.

teach.model: Sound travels at a set speed, so when an aircraft is faster than sound the air cannot get out of the way gradually. It is compressed in a very thin layer called a shock wave. Pressure, temperature and density jump up, and the flow behind a normal shock is slower than sound.

stages.title: Boundary layers and flow separation
stages.hook: The air touching a wing's skin is stuck to it, yet a metre away it moves at 200 m/s. How does the flow connect these, and why can it suddenly leave the surface?
explain: Air is viscous, so at the surface the fluid has zero speed relative to the wing (the no-slip condition). Within a thin region called the boundary layer the speed rises from zero to the free-stream value. The Reynolds number Re = ρvL ÷ μ compares inertial to viscous effects, with μ the dynamic viscosity (about 1.789 × 10⁻⁵ Pa·s for air at 15 °C).

The boundary layer begins laminar (smooth layers) and can change to turbulent (mixing). On a flat plate this happens near Re_x ≈ 5 × 10⁵. A turbulent layer has more skin friction but carries more energy near the wall, so it resists separation better. Dimples on a golf ball use this: a turbulent layer lets the flow stay attached longer and cuts pressure drag.

When pressure rises along the flow (an adverse pressure gradient), the slow air near the wall can stop or reverse and the flow separates from the surface. On a wing this happens as the angle of attack grows: lift falls and drag rises. This is a stall. Vortex generators, slats and flaps energise the flow to delay separation.

example.q: At what distance x from the leading edge of a flat plate does the boundary layer reach Re_x = 5×10⁵ in air at 10 m/s? (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, μ = 1.789×10⁻⁵ Pa·s)
steps: Re_x = ρvx ÷ μ, so x = Re_x μ ÷ (ρv).

analogies.sea: Water at a river bank is nearly still while the middle flows fast.
analogies.home: Dust stays on the blades of a fan: the air layer on the surface barely moves.
analogies.sport: A cyclist drafting behind a rider in a slow, dragging air layer saves effort.
analogies.tech: Golf balls have dimples because a rough surface triggers a turbulent layer.

stages.mnemonic: Stuck at the wall, fast far away; laminar slips, turbulent clings; adverse gradients split.
terms: The thin layer next to a surface where viscosity slows the flow.
Re = ρvL/μ, ratio of inertial to viscous effects.
Smooth flow in layers with low friction.
Irregular, mixing flow with higher skin friction.
The boundary layer detaches from the surface, causing stall and pressure drag.

misc.wrong: A turbulent boundary layer is always worse than a laminar one.
misc.right: Turbulent layers cause more skin friction but resist separation better. For a golf ball or a wing at high angle, turbulence can reduce total drag or delay a stall.

stages.limits: Transition depends on roughness, pressure gradient and turbulence in the free stream, not on Re alone. The 5×10⁵ value is a typical flat-plate guide.

Laminar
Both equally

questions.q: Why is a golf ball dimpled?

To look good on the golf course and for no other reason
To add weight so the ball lands more steadily
To reduce lift so that the ball does not float away
questions.why: A turbulent layer stays attached further round the ball, shrinking the wake.

questions.q: A wing's angle of attack becomes very large and the flow separates from the upper surface. What happens to lift?

It doubles because more air is pushed down
It stays the same, only drag changes

questions.q: What causes flow to separate from a surface?
o: An adverse pressure gradient acting on slow air near the wall
A favourable pressure gradient pushing the flow along
Perfect inviscid flow with nothing at all to slow it
Zero viscosity in the thin layer next to the wall
questions.why: Rising pressure along the flow decelerates the low-energy air near the wall until it reverses.

questions.q: Put these in order along a flat plate from the leading edge.
questions.why: The flow begins attached and laminar, transitions at Re_x ≈ 5×10⁵, then becomes turbulent.

questions.q: Why do vortex generators (small fins on a wing) help delay a stall?
questions.model: Vortex generators stir faster air from outside down into the slow boundary layer. The extra energy lets it fight the adverse pressure gradient longer, so separation is delayed.
questions.why: Mixing energises the boundary layer.

panel.q: Two flat plates are tested: plate A at 10 m/s and plate B at 20 m/s in the same air. Where does transition occur?
o: Closer to the leading edge on plate B
Further back from the leading edge on plate B
At exactly the same place on both plates
Never on plate B, which stays smooth
panel.why: x = Re μ/(ρv), so doubling v halves the distance to transition.

panel.q: Which statement correctly links skin friction and pressure drag for a bluff body?

Pressure drag and skin friction are the same thing
Separation lowers every kind of drag at once, including friction
Skin friction is zero for every bluff body
panel.why: Total drag depends on the balance between friction and the size of the wake.

panel.q: Why does the drag on a streamlined body come mainly from skin friction, while a flat plate facing the flow has mostly pressure drag?
panel.model: A streamlined body keeps the flow attached so the wake is small and pressure drag is low; skin friction dominates. A plate facing the flow separates the flow into a large wake, so the pressure difference between front and back gives most of the drag.
panel.why: Drag type depends on how much the flow separates.

teach.topic: What a boundary layer is and why flow separates
teach.model: Air next to a surface is stuck to it, so there is a thin layer where the speed rises from zero to the outside speed. This is the boundary layer. If the pressure rises along the surface, the slow air near the wall can stop and reverse, so the flow separates and the wing stalls.

stages.title: Aircraft stability and control
stages.hook: An aircraft can be flown 'hands off' for minutes and recover from gusts, but some fighter jets are designed to fall out of the sky without computer help. What is the design trade?
explain: Static stability is the initial tendency after a disturbance: stable if it produces a restoring moment. For pitch, the aircraft is statically stable if the centre of gravity (CG) is ahead of the neutral point (NP), where the pitching moment does not change with angle of attack. The static margin is (x_NP − x_CG) ÷ c̄, expressed as a fraction of the mean chord; typical values are a few percent to about 25%.

Dynamic stability concerns how the motion develops in time. The long-period phugoid is a slow exchange of height and speed with a period of roughly T ≈ π√2 · V ÷ g. The short-period mode is a rapid pitch oscillation that must be well damped. In the lateral motions, Dutch roll is a coupled yaw-roll oscillation, and spiral mode is a slow divergence of bank.

The horizontal tail has a tail volume coefficient V_H = S_t l_t ÷ (S c̄), where S_t is tail area, l_t the tail arm, S wing area and c̄ mean chord. A larger V_H makes the aircraft more stable in pitch. High stability means less manoeuvrability, so relaxed-stability fighters use fly-by-wire computers to keep the aircraft controllable.

example.q: An aircraft has mean chord 2 m. Its neutral point is 1.10 m behind the wing's leading-edge reference and the CG is 0.80 m behind it. Find the static margin.

analogies.sea: A boat with a low centre of mass rights itself; a top-heavy boat flips.
analogies.sport: A kayak is stable when wide and slow to turn; a racing kayak is narrow, quick and tippy.
analogies.home: A weather vane points into the wind because its tail is behind the pivot.
analogies.tech: A gyro-stabilised drone keeps level using continuous corrections.

stages.mnemonic: CG ahead of NP: stable. Behind it: unstable. The static margin is the distance, over chord.
terms: The CG position at which the aircraft is neutrally stable in pitch.
A slow oscillation exchanging height and speed.
A coupled yaw and roll oscillation.

misc.wrong: A statically stable aircraft always returns to its original flight condition.
misc.right: Static stability only gives a restoring tendency at first. Dynamic behaviour (damping) decides whether the motion dies away or grows.

stages.limits: Formulas such as the phugoid period are approximations that assume simple conditions. Full stability analysis uses linearised equations of motion with many derivatives.

A control surface on the tail
questions.why: The phugoid is a long-period mode with nearly constant angle of attack.

questions.q: A cargo is loaded far aft and the aircraft becomes difficult to control. Explain why using the idea of the static margin.
questions.model: Loading aft moves the CG backward toward or past the neutral point. The static margin shrinks or becomes negative, so the restoring moment in pitch is weak or reversed and the aircraft is hard or impossible to control.
questions.why: Pitch stability needs the CG ahead of the neutral point.

panel.q: An aircraft is statically stable but its oscillation slowly grows larger. How would you describe it?

Statically unstable, because it returns toward trim at first
Neutrally stable, since the size never changes
Not an aircraft, because it is not steady
panel.why: A restoring tendency can overshoot and build up if damping is too low.

panel.q: Why are the horizontal tail's area and arm both important for pitch stability?

Only the area matters, never the arm

panel.why: Tail volume coefficient combines area and arm because moment is force times distance.

panel.q: Why do airliners use yaw dampers even though they have fins?
panel.model: At cruise a swept-wing airliner's Dutch roll can be lightly damped, producing a yaw-roll wobble that is uncomfortable. A yaw damper uses sensors and the rudder to add damping and suppress it.
panel.why: Static stability from the fin does not guarantee good damping.

teach.topic: Static stability and the static margin
teach.model: An aircraft is stable in pitch if it tends to return to its original angle after a gust. This works when the centre of gravity is ahead of the neutral point. The distance between them, divided by the mean chord, is the static margin; bigger margin means more stability but less agility.

stages.title: Aircraft structures and stress analysis
stages.hook: A wing bends upward by a metre or more in turbulence on some airliners and does not break. How do engineers know how much load a structure can take?
explain: Normal stress is σ = F ÷ A and shear stress is τ = F ÷ A acting along the surface. Strain is the relative change in length, ε = ΔL ÷ L. In the elastic range stress is proportional to strain (σ = Eε, with E the Young's modulus). Aluminium alloys have E ≈ 70 GPa. Beyond the yield stress the material deforms permanently.

For a beam such as a wing spar, the bending stress at distance c from the neutral axis is σ = M c ÷ I, where M is the bending moment and I the second moment of area. For a rectangle of width b and height h, I = b h³ ÷ 12. Doubling the depth h raises I by a factor of 8, which is why deep spars are efficient. The fuselage is a pressure vessel: for a thin-walled cylinder, hoop stress is σ = p r ÷ t.

Aircraft are designed using a flight envelope (V-n diagram) giving the load factors expected at each speed. The limit load is the highest expected in service; the ultimate load is typically 1.5 times that. Fatigue from repeated loading and corrosion mean structures follow damage-tolerance rules with inspection schedules.

example.q: A rectangular spar section has b = 0.05 m, h = 0.10 m and carries a bending moment of 2000 N·m. Find the maximum bending stress.

analogies.home: A plank stands on its edge is stiffer than flat, as I grows with the cube of depth.
analogies.city: Bridge girders are deep at the middle for the same reason.
analogies.sport: A fishing rod bends when loaded and springs back if not overstressed.
analogies.farm: A tall narrow beam in a barn roof carries more load than the same wood laid flat.

stages.mnemonic: Stress is force over area; bending stress is M c over I; hoop is p r over t.
terms: Force per unit area, in pascals.
E, the ratio of stress to strain in the elastic range.
The stress at which permanent deformation begins.
Ratio of ultimate load to limit load, typically 1.5.

misc.wrong: A structure fails only when the load is above its static strength.
misc.right: Repeated loads can cause fatigue cracks that fail a part at stresses well below the static strength.

stages.limits: Closed-form formulas assume simple shapes and linear elastic materials. Real design uses finite element methods, tests and certification rules.

panel.q: A wing spar is moved from flat to on-edge orientation, with the same cross-section 0.05 m × 0.10 m. The stress for the same moment changes by a factor of

panel.q: Why is the fuselage cross-section usually circular or nearly circular?
panel.model: A pressurised fuselage is a pressure vessel. A circular section carries the internal pressure mainly in tension (hoop stress) and spreads it evenly, avoiding the bending that flat sides would suffer.
panel.why: Round shapes carry pressure efficiently.

stages.title: Gas turbine propulsion
stages.hook: A modern jet engine squeezes air about thirty times before burning fuel in it. Why does squeezing first make the engine so much more efficient?
explain: The ideal gas turbine follows the Brayton cycle: compression, constant-pressure heating, expansion, and exhaust. For an ideal cycle the thermal efficiency is η = 1 − 1 ÷ r_p^((γ−1)/γ), where r_p is the pressure ratio and γ = 1.4. With r_p = 30, η ≈ 0.62. Real engines reach lower values because of component losses, but the trend is clear: higher pressure ratio and higher turbine inlet temperature give better efficiency.

In an isentropic compressor the exit temperature is T₂ = T₁ r_p^((γ−1)/γ). For T₁ = 288.15 K and r_p = 30, T₂ ≈ 761 K. The temperature at the turbine inlet is limited by materials, and engines use cooling air and special alloys. Overall efficiency is the product of thermal efficiency and propulsive efficiency.

Propulsive efficiency is η_p = 2 ÷ (1 + v_e/v₀) for a simple jet, where v_e is the exhaust speed and v₀ the flight speed. It is high when the exhaust speed is close to the flight speed. This is why airliners use high-bypass turbofans (a large mass of air with a modest speed increase) while supersonic aircraft use low-bypass or afterburning engines.

example.q: Find the ideal Brayton thermal efficiency for a pressure ratio of 30 (γ = 1.4).

analogies.sport: A diver coils before a jump: stored compression gives a stronger launch.
analogies.home: A bicycle pump heats up as it compresses air.
analogies.city: A cold-start engine runs better as it warms. A hotter cycle allows more work.
analogies.tech: A turbo in a car engine compresses incoming air to burn more fuel.

stages.mnemonic: Higher pressure ratio, higher efficiency; match jet speed to flight speed for propulsion efficiency.

Compressor exit pressure divided by inlet pressure.
Gas temperature entering the turbine, limited by materials.
Fraction of jet kinetic energy that does useful propulsive work.
Bypass mass flow divided by core mass flow.

misc.wrong: A jet engine is most efficient when the exhaust is as fast as possible.
misc.right: A very fast exhaust wastes kinetic energy. Propulsive efficiency is highest when exhaust speed is only a little above flight speed.

stages.limits: The ideal cycle ignores losses in compressor, combustor, turbine and nozzle. Real efficiencies are lower, and the numbers here are for illustration.

The colour of the fuel burned in the engine

It burns no fuel at all while flying
It has no turbine, so there is nothing to wear out
It uses wings inside the engine to make extra lift
questions.why: Exhaust speed is close to flight speed, so less kinetic energy is wasted.

questions.q: Why does a higher pressure ratio improve ideal efficiency?
o: The gas is expanded through a larger temperature drop in the turbine

stages.title: Rotorcraft flight dynamics
stages.hook: If a helicopter's engine fails, it can still land safely. How can the rotor keep turning with no power?
explain: In hover, the rotor thrust equals the weight. Momentum theory gives the induced velocity v_i = √(T ÷ (2ρA)) and the ideal induced power P_i = T v_i. Real rotors need more: the figure of merit FM = ideal power ÷ actual power is typically about 0.6 to 0.75. For a hover with T = 19 620 N, ρ = 1.225 kg/m³ and A = 113.1 m², v_i = 8.41 m/s and P_i ≈ 165 kW.

In forward flight the rotor tilts so a part of its thrust provides propulsion. Translational lift is the extra efficiency gained as the rotor moves into undisturbed air, so less power is needed at moderate speed than in hover. Near the ground, ground effect also reduces the induced velocity. Control is by collective pitch (changing all blade angles together to alter thrust) and cyclic pitch (changing each blade's angle with its position to tilt the rotor disk).

In autorotation, the engine is disconnected and air flowing up through the rotor as the helicopter descends keeps it spinning. The stored energy in the rotor is used for a flare at the end to reduce the descent rate for landing. Helicopters are also affected by hazards such as retreating blade stall at high speed and vortex ring state in a steep, slow descent.

example.q: A helicopter has mass 2000 kg and rotor radius 6 m. Find the ideal hover induced power (g = 9.81 m/s², ρ = 1.225 kg/m³).

stages.title: Aircraft systems and avionics
stages.hook: A modern airliner is full of computers, yet the pilot still reads a speed from a simple tube in the airflow. What does the aircraft measure, and how does it decide what to trust?
explain: The pitot-static system measures airspeed and altitude from pressure. A pitot tube faces the flow and senses total pressure p₀; static ports sense ambient pressure p. The difference is the dynamic pressure q = p₀ − p = ½ρv², so v = √(2q ÷ ρ). The altimeter converts static pressure to height using the standard atmosphere, so it must be set to a reference pressure.

Navigation uses inertial sensors, radio aids and satellite systems (GNSS). A GNSS receiver measures the travel time of signals from several satellites: distance = c × t with c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. It needs at least four satellites to solve for three position coordinates and the receiver clock error. An autopilot compares the measured state with a target and moves control surfaces to reduce the error, using a feedback loop.

Safety-critical systems use redundancy: duplicated or triplicated sensors and computers, with voting. If three independent channels each fail with probability p during a flight, all three fail with probability p³. Designers also guard against common-cause faults that hit all channels at once, such as a blocked pitot tube or a software flaw, so they use different designs and monitor the data for disagreement.

stages.title: Orbital mechanics
stages.hook: To raise a satellite from a low orbit to a high one, you fire your engine twice, and the satellite ends up slower than when it started. How is that possible?
explain: Orbits obey Newton's gravity. For a circular orbit, v = √(GM ÷ r), with GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² for Earth. For any orbit of semi-major axis a, the vis-viva equation gives the speed at distance r: v² = GM(2/r − 1/a). Energy per unit mass is −GM ÷ (2a). Kepler's third law gives the period T = 2π√(a³ ÷ GM). Escape speed is √2 times circular speed at the same radius.

A Hohmann transfer is a two-burn change between circular orbits: an elliptical path whose perigee touches the lower orbit and apogee the higher one. Going from 400 km altitude (r₁ = 6771 km) to geostationary radius (r₂ = 42 164 km), a = (r₁ + r₂)/2 = 24 467 km. The speed at perigee is 10.07 km/s versus 7.67 km/s circular, so Δv₁ ≈ 2.40 km/s. At apogee the speed is 1.62 km/s versus 3.07 km/s circular, so Δv₂ ≈ 1.46 km/s.

The total Δv is about 3.86 km/s and the transfer takes half of the ellipse period, about 5.3 hours. The satellite ends slower in the final orbit because the extra energy goes into height (potential energy). Plane changes are expensive: changing inclination is best done where the speed is lowest. Real missions also include perturbations from Earth's shape, the Moon, the Sun and drag.

stages.title: Rocket propulsion and launch trajectories
stages.hook: A rocket that is 90% propellant by mass still cannot reach orbit in one stage with ordinary propellants. Why do the numbers work out this way?
explain: The thrust of a rocket is F = ṁ v_e + (p_e − p_a)A_e, where ṁ is the propellant flow rate, v_e the exhaust speed and the last term the pressure thrust. Specific impulse Isp = F ÷ (ṁ g₀) in seconds, so v_e = Isp g₀ for the effective exhaust speed. A typical hydrogen-oxygen engine has Isp in vacuum around 450 s; kerosene-oxygen is nearer 350 s.

The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation is Δv = v_e ln(m₀ ÷ m_f), where m₀ is the starting mass and m_f the mass after burning. It is logarithmic, so each extra bit of Δv costs exponentially more propellant. With Isp = 300 s (v_e = 2943 m/s, g₀ = 9.81 m/s²) and a mass ratio of 10, Δv ≈ 6.78 km/s. Reaching low orbit needs about 9.4 km/s, including roughly 1.5 to 2 km/s lost to gravity and drag.

Staging drops empty tanks and engines to avoid carrying them. A launch begins vertically to leave the dense air quickly, then pitches over in a gravity turn to build horizontal speed. Gravity loss is the time spent fighting gravity, so a higher thrust-to-weight ratio reduces it, while aerodynamic loads peak at 'max-Q'. The game's numbers are educational and not for real launch design.
